title: Cores Outlive Containers
story:
From: Tomasz Wierzba
Subject: Eleven days of readings, gone

The core logger kept eleven days of depth readings inside its own container. Tuesday's upgrade replaced that container, and the readings went with it. I am not going to describe how that felt.

Before I trust the new setup, I need proof. From a throwaway container called `core-logger`, write the depth reading of core 0417 into a volume named `ice-cores`. Then delete the container. The reading must still be there afterwards.
objectives: Create a named volume `ice-cores` and mount it at `/data` in a container named `core-logger` (`alpine:3.20`)
startingState: A clean engine: no volumes and no containers.
hints: Anything written in a container's own filesystem is deleted with the container. A named volume is stored separately and outlives it.
Mount the volume with `-v ice-cores:/data` (it is created if missing). Run a one-shot command that writes the file, then remove the container with `docker rm`.

```bash
docker run --name core-logger -v ice-cores:/data alpine:3.20 \
  sh -c 'echo "DEPTH 1450 M" > /data/core-0417.txt'
docker rm core-logger
docker run --rm -v ice-cores:/data alpine:3.20 cat /data/core-0417.txt
```

validation.description: A fresh container mounting `ice-cores` can still read `core-0417.txt` containing `DEPTH 1450 M`

solution: docker run --name core-logger -v ice-cores:/data alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo "DEPTH 1450 M" > /data/core-0417.txt'
debrief: A named volume lives under the engine's control, independent of any container, so removing the container leaves the data alone. Pro tip: `docker rm -v` only removes anonymous volumes; named ones are never deleted unless you run `docker volume rm`.
